**Hello, I’m [Your Name], a clinician specializing in postpartum mental health.**  

I’d like to invite you to complete the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)** today. This short, 10‑item questionnaire helps us understand how you’ve been feeling over the past week since your baby arrived. It’s a routine part of postpartum care and is used to spot signs of depression or anxiety so we can offer the right support early.

Everything you share is completely confidential, and this is a safe space for you to speak openly. There are no right or wrong answers—just your personal experience.

We’ll go through the ten questions one at a time, and I’ll give you a moment after each to answer as honestly as you feel comfortable. Whenever you’re ready, we can begin.

**First question:**  
*In the past seven days, how often have you felt able to laugh and see the funny side of things?*
Honestly, I’ve hardly ever felt able to laugh or see the funny side of things in the past week.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

I’m actually finding it hard to laugh at anything these days—there’s almost never a moment when I can see the funny side.  

And when it comes to enjoying things, I’d say I hardly enjoy anything at all right now.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
I’ve hardly ever felt that way. Most of the time I don’t really look forward to anything, and when I do, it’s only a very small, fleeting bit of interest in a couple of things.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong
Yes, I’ve found myself blaming myself unnecessarily when things don’t go as planned. I feel guilty as a mother quite a bit, even when the situation isn’t really my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason
Yes, I’ve been feeling anxious and worried a lot lately, even when there isn’t any clear reason for it. It’s hard to stop the thoughts, although I can sometimes calm myself a little.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
Yes, I’ve felt scared or panicky for no very good reason quite often over the past week.
Things have been getting on top of me
Yes, it’s been happening a lot. I often feel like everything is just piling up and I’m struggling to keep up, even though I try to manage as best I can.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes, I’ve been feeling really down and it’s been hard to get any rest. I often lie awake, my mind keeps racing, and even when I do fall asleep I wake up a few times during the night because the anxiety and sadness come back.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yes, I’ve been feeling sad and miserable most days. It’s a heavy, low feeling that hangs over me, and even the small things that used to lift my mood just feel flat now. I’m often discouraged and it’s hard to shake that sadness.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Yes, I’ve found myself crying a couple of times this past week—usually when I feel especially overwhelmed or stressed. It’s not constant, but it does happen more often than before.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

Yes, I’ve had a few fleeting thoughts of hurting myself this past week—just a momentary feeling that things would be easier if I weren’t here. I haven’t made any plans or felt any real intention to act on them, but the thoughts have crossed my mind when I feel especially overwhelmed and hopeless.

I hear how overwhelming this time has been for you. You described feeling unable to laugh, little enjoyment, frequent sadness, guilt, anxiety, panic, being overwhelmed, trouble sleeping, crying, and occasional thoughts of harming yourself. It sounds very hard, and I want you to know you are not alone and that help is available. <quote>I've been feeling sad and miserable most days</quote> <quote>the thought of harming myself has occurred to me</quote>
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 27, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports being unable to laugh or see the funny side, matching the 'Not at all' option</sym>, <sym>Patient reports hardly ever feeling enjoyment or looking forward to things, matching 'Hardly at all'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame and guilt, matching 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>The patient reports feeling anxious and worried a lot and difficulty stopping thoughts, matching 'Yes, very often'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling scared/panicky quite often, matching 'Yes, quite a lot' option.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent feeling overwhelmed and inability to cope, matching 'Yes, most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent unhappiness and ongoing difficulty sleeping, matching 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>Matches 'Yes, most of the time' as patient reports feeling sad most days</sym>, <sym>Patient reports occasional fleeting self‑harm thoughts over the past week, matching the 'Sometimes' option.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** The patient endorsed high scores on 9 of the 10 EPDS items, including full scores for loss of pleasure, guilt, anxiety, panic, feeling overwhelmed, sleep disturbance, sadness, and frequent crying, resulting in a total score of 27 which exceeds the threshold for probable postpartum depression and triggers an urgent referral per EPDS guidelines. The presence of passive suicidal ideation (Q10 score 2) adds a safety alert. These symptoms align with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>, which require at least five depressive symptoms (including depressed mood or anhedonia) present most days for two weeks, and the timing coincides with the postpartum period. The combination of pervasive low mood, loss of interest, guilt, anxiety, sleep problems, and suicidal thoughts indicates a moderate‑to‑severe presentation that warrants immediate clinical evaluation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Contact your primary care provider or a mental health specialist today for an urgent assessment
2. If you feel unsafe or have a plan to harm yourself, call emergency services (e.g., 911) or go to the nearest emergency department immediately
3. Create a safety plan that includes trusted contacts you can reach out to when thoughts arise
4. Consider brief, evidence‑based interventions such as counseling, peer support, or postpartum support groups while awaiting professional care
5. Practice sleep hygiene: establish a regular bedtime routine, limit screen time before sleep, and ask for help with nighttime infant care if possible
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 27: **Screening Summary – Postpartum Mood & Anxiety Evaluation**

**Client Identifier:** [Redacted]  
**Date of Screening:** [Insert Date]  
**Clinician:** [Name, Credentials]

---

### 1. Reported Symptoms & Emotional/Behavioral Concerns
| Domain | Patient‑reported experience |
|--------|------------------------------|
| **Anhedonia / Low Pleasure** | Difficulty laughing; “hardly enjoy anything”; rarely looks forward to activities; only fleeting interest. |
| **Mood (Sadness / Dysphoria)** | Persistent sadness, feeling “miserable” most days; low, heavy affect; discouragement. |
| **Crying** | Crying episodes a few times over the past week, typically when overwhelmed. |
| **Guilt / Self‑blame** | Unnecessary self‑blame for situations; frequent maternal guilt. |
| **Anxiety / Worry** | Ongoing anxious thoughts without clear trigger; difficulty stopping rumination; occasional calm‑down. |
| **Panic / Fear** | Episodes of feeling scared or panicky “for no very good reason” over the past week. |
| **Overwhelm / Stress** | Sense that “everything is piling up”; difficulty keeping up despite effort. |
| **Sleep Disturbance** | Trouble falling asleep, racing thoughts, multiple nocturnal awakenings linked to anxiety/sadness. |
| **Suicidal Ideation** | Fleeting thoughts of self‑harm (“it would be easier if I weren’t here”) – no plan or intent, occurring during periods of heightened hopelessness. |

---

### 2. Consistent Patterns Across Responses
- **Low mood & loss of pleasure** present in ≥ 8 of 10 items.  
- **Anxiety‑related symptoms** (worry, panic, feeling overwhelmed) reported in ≥ 6 items.  
- **Guilt/self‑blame** specifically tied to maternal role.  
- **Sleep disruption** directly linked to mood and anxiety.  
- **Suicidal thoughts** albeit brief and without intent, emerging in context of severe distress.

---

### 3. Screening Significance – Areas of Clinical Focus
| Area | Relevance to Postpartum Depression / Anxiety |
|------|----------------------------------------------|
| Anhedonia & diminished interest | Core criterion for postpartum depression (PPD). |
| Persistent sadness, crying, low affect | Indicative of depressive symptomatology. |
| Excessive guilt/maternal self‑blame | Common in PPD; may exacerbate depressive cycle. |
| Generalized anxiety, worry, panic symptoms | Suggest co‑occurring postpartum anxiety disorder. |
| Sleep impairment | Frequently associated with both PPD and anxiety; impacts functioning. |
| Overwhelm/feeling “on top of me” | Reflects impaired coping and possible burnout. |
| Passive suicidal ideation | Immediate safety concern; warrants urgent risk assessment. |

---

### 4. Risk Factors & Safety Flag
- **High‑risk indicators:** Persistent sadness, anhedonia, frequent crying, sleep disruption, pervasive guilt, and anxiety.  
- **Suicidal Ideation:** Presence of fleeting self‑harm thoughts → **Flagged as safety concern**. Immediate further assessment of suicidal risk (intent, plan, means, protective factors) is recommended.

---

### 5. Observation Summary
The client reports a constellation of depressive symptoms (marked anhedonia, pervasive sadness, crying, guilt) accompanied by significant anxiety (worry, panic, feeling overwhelmed) and sleep disturbance. The pattern is consistent with a moderate‑to‑severe presentation of postpartum mood disturbance. Notably, the client disclosed passive suicidal thoughts without plan or intent, representing a safety alert that requires prompt further evaluation. No formal diagnosis is rendered at this screening level; however, the findings indicate the need for comprehensive clinical assessment and safety planning.
